questions.q: Four people are at a gurudwara's langar on a Sunday. Whose activity is seva as the chapter describes it?
questions.a: A student who serves food to visitors and takes nothing
o: A student who serves food to visitors and takes nothing
A cook employed by the gurudwara and paid every month
A vegetable seller who supplies the kitchen for ₹3,000
A visitor who sits down with others and eats a meal there

questions.q:
Neha cooks dinner every evening for her aunt, who is ill. Iqbal, unpaid, cooks every Friday at a mosque's free kitchen for anyone who comes.
(a) Are both activities economic or non-economic? Give the reason.
(b) Which of the two fits better the chapter's description of seva as a way of contributing to society, and why?
questions.a: (a) Both are non-economic: neither generates income or wealth, and each is done out of feelings like love and care. (b) Iqbal's cooking: he serves anyone who comes, not only his own family, without expecting anything in return, which is how the chapter describes seva as contributing to society. Neha's care is for her own family member.
s: Part (a): both non-economic, no income, done out of care
Part (b): Iqbal's, as it serves anyone, contributing to society without expecting a return

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A doctor who runs a paid clinic on weekdays, and treats patients free at a temple's health camp on Sundays expecting nothing in return, is doing seva on Sundays.
Reason (R): Seva is seen in many places, such as temples, gurudwaras, mosques and churches.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Sanjay writes: 'Seva means selfless service, and it is found only at gurudwaras, where langars feed every visitor for free.' Test each part of his statement against the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. Seva does mean selfless service, and langars at gurudwaras do serve food to every visitor for free. But 'only at gurudwaras' is wrong: the chapter says we see seva in many places such as temples, gurudwaras, mosques and churches.
s: Verdict: partly right
Supported: seva is selfless service; langars feed every visitor free
Corrected: seva is seen at temples, gurudwaras, mosques and churches, not only gurudwaras

questions.q: Raman cooks in a langar kitchen and is paid a monthly salary by the committee that runs it. Even though the visitors eat for free, by the chapter's definitions Raman's cooking is a(n) ___ activity.
questions.a: economic

questions.q: A school club wants to run a 'seva stall' at its annual fair. Which plan fits the chapter's meaning of seva?
questions.a: Serve free water to every visitor, asking nothing back
o: Serve free water to every visitor, asking nothing back
Serve free water only to the students of their own school
Serve free water to those who first buy a fair ticket
Serve water to all visitors and charge ₹5 for a glass

questions.q:
From a school magazine: 'On the festival day, 40 volunteers ran the community kitchen beside the temple from 7 a.m. to 3 p.m. They worked in two equal shifts of 20 volunteers each. The kitchen served 2,400 visitors, and no one was asked to pay. The flour, rice and vegetables were given by families of the neighbourhood.'
(a) How many hours did each volunteer work, and how many volunteer-hours were given in all?
(b) On average, how many visitors were served per volunteer?
(c) Is the volunteers' work an economic or a non-economic activity? Give the chapter's reason.
(d) Next year the organisers plan to hire 10 cooks at ₹500 a day each, along with the volunteers. Work out what this will cost, and say whether the cooks' work will be seva.
questions.a: (a) 7 a.m. to 3 p.m. is 8 hours; two equal shifts give 4 hours each; 40 x 4 = 160 volunteer-hours. (b) 2,400 / 40 = 60 visitors per volunteer. (c) Non-economic: the volunteers earn no income and serve without expecting anything in return; it is seva, selfless service. (d) 10 x ₹500 = ₹5,000. The cooks' work will not be seva: they are paid a daily wage, so it is an economic activity, while the volunteers' work stays seva.
s: Part (a): 4 hours each, 160 volunteer-hours
Part (b): 60 visitors per volunteer
Part (c): non-economic, no income, nothing expected in return
Part (d): ₹5,000; paid cooks do economic work, not seva

questions.q:
A village temple runs a free community kitchen. Every day 25 volunteers cook and serve, and about 300 people eat there; the ingredients, worth ₹4,200 a day, are given by village families. At the panchayat meeting a member proposes: 'The kitchen earns nothing, so either close it or charge ₹14 a plate so that it pays for itself.'
(a) What do the ingredients cost per meal?
(b) Is the volunteers' work economic or non-economic? Does 'it earns nothing' show that it has no value? Use the chapter.
(c) If a ₹14 charge were brought in, which part of the chapter's description of a langar-style kitchen would the kitchen no longer match?
(d) Decide whether the panchayat should keep the kitchen free, giving two things the village would lose if it closed or began charging.
questions.a: (a) ₹4,200 / 300 = ₹14 per meal. (b) Non-economic: the volunteers earn no income and serve without expecting anything in return; it is seva. 'Earns nothing' is true of every non-economic activity, but the chapter says the value such activities generate is important in our lives, so earning nothing does not mean having no value. (c) A langar serves food to every visitor for free; with a charge, only those who pay would eat, so it would no longer serve every visitor free. (d) Keep it free. Closing or charging would lose a way for the village to contribute to society without expecting anything in return, and the sense of satisfaction and gratitude that such seva fosters in those who take part; with a charge, visitors who cannot pay would also no longer be served.
s: Part (a): ₹14 per meal
Part (b): non-economic seva; no income does not mean no value, as the chapter says its value is important
Part (c): it would no longer serve food to every visitor for free
Part (d): decision to keep it free
Part (d): two losses (contribution to society with no return expected; satisfaction and gratitude; visitors who cannot pay)

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column A with the term from the chapter in Column B.
Column A: 1. A visitor eats a free meal at a gurudwara's kitchen  2. A volunteer serves meals there and wants nothing back  3. A farm labourer receives mangoes for tilling a field  4. A patient pays a doctor for advice
Column B: a. payment in kind (a non-cash payment for work)  b. fee (a payment for professional advice or services)  c. langar (a community kitchen serving food free to every visitor)  d. seva (selfless service)
True or False: 'Since seva earns no income, the chapter treats it as less important than economic activities.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter places seva under 'The Importance of Non-Economic Activities' and says that while non-economic activities may not involve money, the value they generate is important in our lives; seva fosters satisfaction and gratitude and contributes to society without expecting anything in return.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: the value non-economic activities generate is important; seva brings satisfaction, gratitude and contributes to society

questions.q: After helping at a church's free eye camp for a day, Arun says, 'Seeing people who cannot read their own letters made me thankful for my own eyes.' Which part of the chapter's description of seva does his remark show most directly?
questions.a: It fosters gratitude for what we have
o: It fosters gratitude for what we have
It contributes to society, expecting nothing
It is service done for an employer's wage
It gives a payment in kind of good health

questions.q: Show that the chapter's method of working out value addition, used for Rajesh's chair, cannot be applied to the meals served at a langar.
questions.a: The method needs a selling price and the cost of the raw material: value added = selling price minus raw-material cost, as in ₹1,000 - ₹600 = ₹400. A langar serves food to every visitor for free, so there is no selling price. With no selling price there is nothing to subtract the cost from, so the method cannot be used; the chapter instead says the value non-economic activities generate is important in our lives.
s: The method needs a selling price minus a raw-material cost
Langar meals are free to every visitor, so there is no selling price
No selling price, so the subtraction cannot be done; the value lies elsewhere

questions.q:
Mrs D'Souza is a nurse at a hospital and receives a monthly salary. Every Sunday she helps serve a free meal to elderly people at her church, asking nothing in return.
(a) Classify her two activities as economic or non-economic.
(b) Which one is seva as the chapter describes it, and why?
questions.a: (a) Nursing for a salary is economic; serving the free Sunday meal is non-economic. (b) The Sunday meal, because it is selfless service seen at a church, given without expecting anything in return.
s: Part (a): nursing economic; Sunday meal non-economic
Part (b): the Sunday meal, selfless service with nothing expected in return

questions.q: Pooja serves food every Sunday at her gurudwara's langar and asks for nothing. Which change would stop her work there from being seva as the chapter describes it?
questions.a: She asks the committee for ₹200 each day she serves
o: She asks the committee for ₹200 each day she serves
She starts serving at a church's free kitchen instead
She serves only on festival days instead of weekly
She serves twice as many visitors as before each day

questions.q: Compare a volunteer serving food at a langar with a cook employed at a restaurant under these heads: (a) payment received, (b) who is served and whether they pay, (c) what is expected in return, (d) the group each activity belongs to. Then (e) analyse what each contributes, using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) The volunteer receives nothing; the restaurant cook is paid by the employer. (b) The volunteer serves every visitor, all for free; the cook serves customers who pay for their food. (c) The volunteer expects nothing in return; the cook works in exchange for money. (d) The volunteer's work is non-economic (seva, selfless service); the cook's is economic. (e) The cook's work has value in terms of money; the volunteer's seva contributes to society, and the chapter says such practices foster a sense of satisfaction and gratitude for what we have.
s: (a) No payment versus pay from an employer
(b) Every visitor free versus paying customers
(c) Nothing expected versus work for money
(d) Non-economic seva versus economic
(e) Money value versus contribution to society, satisfaction and gratitude

questions.q:
A residents' committee is planning a free community meal for 300 people at a festival. Plan A: hire a caterer, who will cook and serve for ₹18,000. Plan B: residents cook and serve together; the ingredients, costing ₹9,000, are given by the residents themselves. The committee's stated aim is: 'Residents contribute to the community without expecting anything in return.'
(a) In which plan is someone paid for the work? Classify that person's activity.
(b) Work out the cost per person under each option.
(c) Under Plan B, 20 residents would cook and serve for 5 hours each. How many hours of service is that in all?
(d) Which plan meets the committee's aim? Justify using the chapter's description of seva.
questions.a: (a) Plan A: the caterer is paid ₹18,000 for cooking and serving, an economic activity. (b) A: ₹18,000 / 300 = ₹60 per person; B: ₹9,000 / 300 = ₹30 per person. (c) 20 x 5 = 100 hours. (d) Plan B: the residents themselves serve without being paid, which is seva, contributing to society without expecting anything in return. In Plan A the work is done for payment, so the residents would only be paying for the meal, not contributing service.
s: Part (a): the caterer in Plan A; economic activity
Part (b): ₹60 and ₹30 per person
Part (c): 100 hours
Part (d): Plan B, unpaid service with nothing expected in return

questions.q:
Ruby says: 'A visitor who eats at a langar is doing seva.'
(a) Is Ruby right? Give a reason.
(b) Who at a langar is doing seva, then?
questions.a: (a) No. The visitor receives the free food; seva is selfless service given to others, and eating a meal is not service to anyone. (b) The people who cook and serve the food for free, without expecting anything in return.
s: Part (a): No, the visitor receives the service and does not give it
Part (b): those who cook and serve for free

questions.q: Which two features of seva, as the chapter describes it, place it among non-economic activities? Illustrate each with a langar, and then say what the chapter says such practices give, instead of money.
questions.a: First, seva involves no money for the service: langars serve food to every visitor for free. Second, it is done without expecting anything in return: those who cook and serve are selfless and ask nothing back. Instead of money, such practices foster a sense of satisfaction and gratitude for what we have and are a way of contributing to society.
s: Feature 1: no money involved (free food for every visitor)
Feature 2: done without expecting anything in return (selfless service)
Instead of money: satisfaction and gratitude, a contribution to society

questions.q:
A gurudwara's langar serves 800 visitors on one day. The ingredients cost ₹12,000, all paid from donations, and volunteers cook and serve.
(a) What did the meals cost per visitor?
(b) The next day the committee decides to charge each visitor that amount, while the same volunteers go on serving unpaid. Is the volunteers' own work still unpaid service, and does the kitchen still match the chapter's description of a langar? Explain.
questions.a: (a) ₹12,000 / 800 = ₹15 per visitor. (b) The volunteers' work is still unpaid, selfless service: they expect nothing in return, so it stays non-economic. But the kitchen no longer matches the chapter's langar, which serves food to every visitor for free; now only those who pay ₹15 eat.
s: Part (a): ₹15 per visitor
Part (b): volunteers still give unpaid service, but the kitchen no longer serves every visitor free

questions.q: On a Sunday, 60 residents of Sector 4 clean their lane and park together, unpaid. The residents' association pays two of them ₹300 each to carry the filled bags to the municipal dump. Which statement fits the chapter?
questions.a: The joint clean-up is non-economic; the two paid carriers do economic work
o: The joint clean-up is non-economic; the two paid carriers do economic work
The whole drive becomes economic, because two of the people were paid money
The whole drive stays non-economic, since all of it was done for the community
The drive is value addition, because the lane and park are worth more now

questions.q:
In Gandhi Nagar every family keeps its own home and courtyard spotless, but no one ever cleans the street or the park, which are full of litter.
(a) Which part of the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan, as the chapter describes it, is missing in Gandhi Nagar?
(b) Using the chapter's chain from a clean home to a clean nation, explain why clean homes alone are not enough.
questions.a: (a) The coming together: people have also come together to clean up streets, roads, parks and other public places, and Gandhi Nagar has no such joint effort. (b) The chapter says individual cleaning of homes and joint cleaning of public places together lead to a clean home, neighbourhood, society and nation; with only homes clean, the chain stops at the home and the neighbourhood stays dirty.
s: Part (a): people coming together to clean streets, roads, parks and public places
Part (b): both efforts together lead to a clean neighbourhood, society and nation; homes alone stop at the home

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The chapter presents the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan as an example of collective community participation.
Reason (R): Under the Abhiyan, people have come together to clean up streets, roads, parks and other public places.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: At a colony clean-up drive, 120 residents work without pay, and 6 municipal sweepers, who are paid a monthly salary, work alongside them. The number of people at the drive doing an economic activity is ___.

Kiran says: 'As the chapter describes it, the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan is not only about cleaning public places; what each family does to keep its own home and surroundings clean is part of it too.' Check her claim against the chapter.
questions.a: Yes, she is right. The chapter says the Abhiyan is based on the collective efforts of all Indian citizens: individually, we keep our homes and surroundings clean, and people have also come together to clean up streets, roads, parks and other public places. Together, these efforts lead to a clean home, neighbourhood, society and nation, so home cleaning is part of it.
s: Verdict: Yes, the claim is right
The chapter names individual cleaning of homes and surroundings as part of the effort
Individual and joint efforts together lead to a clean home, neighbourhood, society and nation

questions.q:
For Van Mahotsav, a school's eco-club keeps this record of saplings planted:
Class 6A students: 36
Class 6B students: 40
Class 6C students: 28
Parents and neighbours: 46
Three months later, 120 of the saplings are still alive.
(a) How many saplings were planted in all?
(b) What percentage of them survived?
(c) Next year there are two plans. Plan 1: students alone plant 300 saplings in the school grounds, where they can water them daily; about 60% are expected to survive. Plan 2: students, parents and neighbours plant 200 saplings along the village road, and families nearby will water them; about 80% are expected to survive. How many surviving trees does each plan give?
(d) The school wants many surviving trees and also wants to celebrate Van Mahotsav as the chapter describes it. Which plan should it choose? Justify using your answers and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 36 + 40 + 28 + 46 = 150. (b) 120 / 150 x 100 = 80%. (c) Plan 1: 60% of 300 = 180 trees; Plan 2: 80% of 200 = 160 trees. (d) Either, if both sides are weighed. Plan 2: the chapter describes Van Mahotsav as bringing members of the community together for tree plantation drives to promote awareness about the value of trees and forest conservation, and Plan 2 involves parents and neighbours; it gives 20 fewer surviving trees. Plan 1 gives 20 more surviving trees, but with students alone it brings far less of the community together.
s: Part (a): 150 saplings
Part (b): 80%
Part (c): 180 and 160 surviving trees
Part (d): a choice weighing 20 more trees against bringing the community together

questions.q: The chapter's closing summary says non-economic activities contribute to social welfare, personal wellbeing and the overall quality of life. Justify this with examples from the chapter: use the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan, Van Mahotsav and seva, and show for each what it gives back even though no one is paid.
questions.a: Swachh Bharat Abhiyan: citizens' collective efforts, at home and in streets, roads and parks, lead to a clean home, neighbourhood, society and nation, which improves the quality of life for everyone. Van Mahotsav: communities come together for tree plantation drives and spread awareness of the value of trees and the conservation of forests, a gain for society as a whole. Seva: langars serve food to every visitor for free (social welfare), and such practices foster a sense of satisfaction and gratitude in those who take part (personal wellbeing). In all three no one earns income, yet each adds value to people's lives, which is the chapter's point that non-economic activities matter.
s: Swachh Bharat: clean surroundings from home to nation, better quality of life
Van Mahotsav: plantation drives and awareness of trees and forest conservation
Seva: free food for every visitor, a contribution to social welfare
Seva: satisfaction and gratitude, personal wellbeing
No income in any of them, yet value is added to life

questions.q: A town plans two events for the same week. Event X: volunteers from every ward plant 500 saplings together in a day. Event Y: a nursery sells 500 saplings to residents at ₹40 each. Which statement fits the chapter?
questions.a: Only X is collective participation, like Van Mahotsav
o: Only X is collective participation, like Van Mahotsav
Both are like Van Mahotsav, as both bring 500 trees
Only Y is non-economic, as saplings change hands in it
Neither counts, since trees do not add value to a town

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. The chapter gives both the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan and Van Mahotsav as examples of collective community participation.
2. As the chapter describes it, Van Mahotsav is mainly a drive to clean streets, roads and parks.
3. According to the chapter, the only purpose of Van Mahotsav is to plant as many trees as possible.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 only
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: True or False: 'A Van Mahotsav drive in which a nursery is paid to supply the saplings can still be collective community participation as the chapter describes it, if the residents come together to plant them.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter describes Van Mahotsav as bringing members of the community together for tree plantation drives. The nursery's sale of saplings is an economic activity, but the residents planting them together, unpaid, is still the community participation the chapter describes.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: residents coming together to plant is the participation; buying saplings is a separate, economic activity

questions.q: Write a short news report (three or four sentences) about an imaginary collective community activity in a town. Then say which of the chapter's two examples of community participation it is most like, and why it is a non-economic activity.
questions.a: Any fitting report, for example: 'On Saturday, 80 residents of Shanti Nagar met at the lake. Families, shopkeepers and students cleared plastic from the banks and swept the paths to the temple and the school. No one was paid; tea was shared by the residents.' It is most like the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan: citizens joining collective efforts to clean public places. It is non-economic because it generates no income for those taking part and is done for the community, not for money.
s: A report showing many people working together for a shared goal
Correctly linked to the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan or Van Mahotsav
Explains it is non-economic: no income, done for the community

questions.q: An eco-club is choosing a plan for Van Mahotsav. Which plan matches the chapter's description of it best?
questions.a: Students and neighbours plant saplings and learn why trees matter
o: Students and neighbours plant saplings and learn why trees matter
The club pays a nursery to plant 200 saplings while students watch
Students sell saplings at a fair to raise money for school repairs
Students and neighbours sweep the streets, roads and parks together

questions.q:
A housing society holds two Sunday events. Event 1: residents clear plastic from the lake bank and sweep the paths. Event 2: residents plant 60 saplings and the children make posters on why trees and forests must be conserved.
(a) Which of the chapter's two examples of community participation is each event most like?
(b) The organisers say the two events have the same aim. Using the chapter, explain how their aims differ.
questions.a: (a) Event 1 is most like the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan; Event 2 is most like Van Mahotsav. (b) The Swachh Bharat Abhiyan aims to keep our surroundings clean; Van Mahotsav aims to promote awareness about the value of trees and the conservation of forests. Both bring people together, but for different aims.
s: Part (a): Event 1 like Swachh Bharat Abhiyan, Event 2 like Van Mahotsav
Part (b): clean surroundings versus awareness of the value of trees and forest conservation

questions.q:
At a village fair: (i) a potter sells pots she made from clay that cost her ₹200, taking ₹650 in all; (ii) after the fair, 30 villagers sweep the fair ground together, unpaid; (iii) a ticket clerk is paid ₹500 by the fair committee for the day's work.
(a) What value has the potter added?
(b) Classify (ii) and (iii) as economic or non-economic, and name the form of payment in (iii).
(c) Which of the three shows the chapter's idea of value addition, and why only that one?
(d) The chapter is titled 'The Value of Work'. Using the fair, explain how the value of work is shown for economic activities.
(e) Explain how the villagers' sweeping also has value, even though it earns nothing.
questions.a: (a) ₹650 - ₹200 = ₹450, the value of her skill, time and effort. (b) (ii) Non-economic: unpaid, done together for the village. (iii) Economic: the clerk is paid ₹500 by the committee for a specific period (the day), which is a wage. (c) Only the potter's: she transforms clay into pots, and value is added in transforming something into another form; the clerk and the sweepers transform nothing for sale. (d) Economic activities have value in terms of money: the potter's ₹450 of value added and the clerk's ₹500 wage. (e) The chapter says that while non-economic activities may not involve money, the value they generate is important in our lives: the villagers' joint sweeping is collective community participation that keeps their shared surroundings clean.
s: (a) ₹450 value added
(b) Sweeping non-economic; clerk economic, paid a wage
(c) Only the potter transforms something into another form
(d) Economic work's value shown in money (value added, wage)
(e) Unpaid joint sweeping still generates value important in our lives (clean shared surroundings)

questions.q:
From a ward newsletter: 'Last Saturday, 150 residents of Ward 12 came together to clean three parks and two kilometres of road, and collected 900 kg of waste. Before the drive, each household had cleaned its own home and courtyard. The municipality's 25 sanitation workers, who are paid every month, then took the waste away. By Wednesday, a few households had again thrown waste at the road corner.'
(a) On average, how much waste did each resident collect?
(b) Classify the residents' work and the sanitation workers' work as economic or non-economic, with a reason for each.
(c) The newsletter's headline is 'Ward 12 shows the Swachh Bharat spirit'. Judge how far the headline is fair, using one detail from the extract that supports it, one that weakens it, and the chapter's description of the Abhiyan.
questions.a: (a) 900 / 150 = 6 kg per resident. (b) The residents' work is non-economic: they are not paid and work together for their surroundings. The sanitation workers' work is economic: they are paid a monthly salary for it. (c) Largely fair, with a reservation. The chapter describes the Abhiyan as the collective efforts of citizens: individually keeping homes and surroundings clean and coming together to clean streets, roads and parks. Supporting: each household cleaned its own home and courtyard and 150 residents together cleaned three parks and two kilometres of road. Weakening: a few households threw waste at the road corner again, so not all citizens kept their surroundings clean. A judgement either way is accepted if it uses one detail on each side.
s: Part (a): 6 kg per resident
Part (b): residents non-economic (unpaid); sanitation workers economic (salaried)
Part (c): a judgement using the chapter's description, a supporting detail (home and joint clean-up) and a weakening one (waste thrown again)

questions.q:
The chapter's summary says non-economic activities contribute to social welfare, personal wellbeing and the overall quality of life.
(a) After a month of weekend clean-ups, a volunteer says, 'I feel calmer and prouder of myself.' Which of the three does her remark show, and why?
(b) A cleaner neighbourhood helps everyone who lives there. Name one of the other two that it adds to, and explain.
questions.a: (a) Personal wellbeing: the gain she describes is her own feeling, felt by the person who takes part. (b) Either social welfare or the overall quality of life, with a reason: the benefit of a clean neighbourhood is shared by the whole community (social welfare), or it makes daily life better for everyone living there (quality of life).
s: Part (a): personal wellbeing, as it is her own feeling
Part (b): social welfare or quality of life, with a reason based on a shared benefit

questions.q: How does a Swachh Bharat clean-up by residents differ from a langar, as the chapter presents the two?
questions.a: One is many people's joint effort; the other is seva serving free food
o: One is many people's joint effort; the other is seva serving free food
The clean-up is an economic activity; the langar is a non-economic one
Only the langar adds to the quality of life; the clean-up adds nothing
The clean-up is seva at a place of worship; the langar is a civic drive

questions.q: The chapter discusses the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan and Van Mahotsav together under 'The strength of community participation'. State two features, from the chapter, that the two examples share, and say whether taking part in them is an economic or a non-economic activity, with a reason.
questions.a: First, both bring people together: under the Abhiyan people have come together to clean up streets, roads, parks and other public places; Van Mahotsav brings members of the community together for tree plantation drives. Second, the chapter calls both examples of collective community participation (the Abhiyan is based on the collective efforts of all citizens; Van Mahotsav is 'another example of collective community participation'). Taking part in them is a non-economic activity: people do it for the good of the community, not to earn money.
s: Shared feature 1: people come together (clean-ups; plantation drives)
Shared feature 2: both named as collective community participation
Non-economic activity: done for the community, not for money

questions.q:
Dev argues: 'A Van Mahotsav tree plantation drive is an economic activity, because one day the trees will give wood worth a lot of money.'
(a) Is the drive itself economic or non-economic? Give the chapter's test.
(b) What does the chapter say the drive is for, instead of money?
questions.a: (a) Non-economic: the people planting are not paid and the drive generates no income for them; an activity is economic only if it involves money or is done in exchange for money or money's worth. (b) To promote awareness about the value of trees and the conservation of forests, by bringing the community together for tree plantation drives.
s: Part (a): non-economic, as no money or money's worth is exchanged for the planting
Part (b): awareness of the value of trees and forest conservation

questions.a: Village families plant saplings together around the village pond
o: Village families plant saplings together around the village pond
A forest department team, paid monthly, plants saplings by a highway
One family plants a mango sapling in the corner of its own courtyard
